newsitem.title: UK: RALLYING-MCRAE ABSENT BUT NOT FORGOTTEN IN RAC RALLY.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-MCRAE ABSENT BUT NOT FORGOTTEN IN RAC RALLY.

text.p: Former world rally champion Colin McRae will be absent but not forgotten this weekend when the British RAC Rally starts in northern England.

The aggressive Scot, one of an extraordinary dynasty of rally drivers, won the rally last year to become Britain's first world champion. But after a year of spectacular incidents and controversies he will not be taking part because it is a non-championship event.
Instead, McRae hopes his younger brotherAlister can win the famous event to maintain the family's recent good record in the RAC. "He's fast enough, it just depends if his car holds out," said McRae.

Colin McRae, 28, clinched this year's manufacturers' title for his Subaru team by winning the last two world championship events at San Remo and Catalonia, but also made his presence felt during an incident-filled year with some outspoken views on the way his sport is run.

Dubbed by some as the wild man of rallying, McRae has endured several crashes, in the process running up a $750,000 repair bill for his Subaru team, incurring a $75,000 fine for speeding in Argentina, split with his long-serving co-driver Derek Ringer and claimed he has been victimised by the sport's ruling body, the Federation Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA).
"In Argentina, we had all sorts of problems which resulted in me having to fork out $75,000 to the FIA," he recalled during an interview.

"The fine itself was for allegedly speeding in a service area, which no one can prove because they didn't have a speed gun or anything. So, I think it was very unfair and they made an example of me...I was victimised, I think, but that's the way they are. You cannot argue with these people.

"I don't agree with what they did. I think it was far too severe a penalty for what it was and if it had been taken as a proper court case, it would have been flung out straight away which is what makes it so annoying."
For McRae, whose image as a fun-loving speed-freak with homes in Monte Carlo and Verbiers belies his devotion to rallying, the Argentine rally was not the only downturn.
He also crashed in Finland on the 1,000 Lakes rally on a stage he was prevented from preparing for because he had been called before the FIA in Paris.

Asked about his split with Ringer, McRae said: "We worked well together, but obviously every partnership has its problems and the main reason for our split was Derek and Prodrive (the Subaru team entrants).

"Really, I can't say. I am not sure that DR (David Richards, the head of Prodrive and the Subaru team) was too happy with Derek's approach to it all . He felt that he was generally losing interest in the whole thing which you could see he was."

Ringer did not like the demands put upon by the pair's new status as world champions. "It's a very demanding sport," said McRae. "It's very competitive and when things are not going well, it's easy to feel a bit down. But that is the most important time, the time when you have to get back on top again. You always have to remember that."
Next year, McRae will be partnered by Welshman Nicky Grist who is currently co-driver to four times world champion Juha Kankkunen of Finland.

Grist knows all about pressure and expects to be able to help McRae with his consistency. "He is very fast," said Grist. "But I think I can help make sure he gets to the end of the rallies -- I think that will be my main aim in 1997."
